units.title: Hello, Fortran!
units.summary: Write your first Fortran program and print text and numbers with print and simple formats.

lesson.md: Fortran is one of the oldest programming languages, and scientists and engineers still use it for fast number crunching. Every program starts with `program` and a name, and it ends with `end program` and the same name.

lesson.code:
program hello
  implicit none
  print '(A)', "Hello, Fortran!"
end program hello

lesson.md: Line by line: `program hello` starts a program called `hello`. `implicit none` tells the compiler that you declare every variable yourself, which you learn in the next unit. Always write it as the second line. `print` writes one line of output. `end program hello` ends the program.

After `print` comes a **format**, then a comma `,` and the values. The format `'(A)'` is a short text in single quotes with parentheses inside. The letter `A` stands for one piece of text. Text values go in double quotes, like `"Hello"`. Every `print` starts a new line.

lesson.code:
program greet
  implicit none
  print '(A)', "Good morning"
  print '(A, A)', "Fortran ", "is fast"
  print '(A)', "Bye"
end program greet
lesson.output:
Good morning
Fortran is fast
Bye

lesson.md: The format `'(A, A)'` has room for two texts. Fortran prints them right next to each other, so the space after `Fortran` comes from the first text. To print a whole number, use `I0`: the letter `I` stands for integer (a whole number), and `0` means "no extra spaces".

lesson.code:
program numbers
  implicit none
  print '(I0)', 2 + 3
  print '(A)', "2 + 3"
  print '(A, I0)', "Answer: ", 6 * 7
end program numbers

lesson.md: Without quotes, `2 + 3` is a calculation and Fortran prints `5`. In quotes, `"2 + 3"` is only text. The star `*` multiplies. A format can mix text and numbers: `'(A, I0)'` prints a text and then a whole number.

You will often see `print *, "Hi"`. The star lets the compiler choose the layout, and it usually adds a space at the start of the line. This course uses formats such as `'(A)'`, so you always know the exact output.

An exclamation mark `!` starts a **comment**: Fortran ignores the rest of the line. Fortran is also not case sensitive, so `PRINT`, `Print` and `print` mean the same. Old programs are often written in capital letters.

lesson.code:
program comments
  implicit none
  ! print '(A)', "Hidden"
  print '(I0)', 10 - 4  ! 6
  PRINT '(A)', "Done"
end program comments

lesson.md: The name after `end program` must be the same as the name after `program`. Every text needs a closing quote, and a comma must separate the format from the values.

card: `program name` … `end program name` frame a program
`print '(A)', "Hi"` prints text and ends the line
`'(I0)'` prints a whole number, `!` starts a comment

exercises.explain: Fortran ignores the case of letters. `PRINT`, `Print` and `print` all work the same way.

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Declare variables of type integer, real, character and logical, and name fixed values with parameter.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a named place for a value. In Fortran you declare every variable at the top of the program: after `implicit none` and before the first statement. `integer :: age` declares a variable `age` for whole numbers. The sign `=` stores a value in it.

lesson.code:
program age_demo
  implicit none
  integer :: age
  age = 36
  print '(A, I0)', "Age: ", age
  age = age + 1
  print '(A, I0)', "Next year: ", age
end program age_demo

lesson.md: `age = age + 1` is not an equation. Fortran first calculates the right side, here `36 + 1`, and then stores the result `37` in the variable on the left.

`integer` holds whole numbers. `real` holds numbers with a decimal point, such as `2.5`. `character(len=5)` holds a text of exactly 5 characters. `logical` holds `.true.` or `.false.`, and the dots belong to the value. You can give a variable a start value in its declaration.

lesson.code:
program types
  implicit none
  integer :: count = 3
  real :: price = 2.5
  character(len=5) :: fruit = "apple"
  logical :: ripe = .true.
  print '(I0)', count
  print '(F0.2)', price
  print '(A)', fruit
  print '(L1)', ripe
end program types

lesson.md: Each type has its own format. `F0.2` prints a real number with 2 digits after the decimal point. `L1` prints a logical value as `T` for true or `F` for false.

A `character(len=10)` variable always holds 10 characters. Shorter text is filled up with spaces at the end, and longer text is cut. `trim(name)` removes the spaces at the end, `//` joins two texts, and `len(name)` gives the length.

lesson.code:
program names
  implicit none
  character(len=10) :: first
  character(len=3) :: short
  first = "Ada"
  short = "Fortran"
  print '(A)', trim(first) // " Lovelace"
  print '(A)', short
  print '(I0)', len(first)
end program names

lesson.md: Add `parameter` to a declaration to make a **named constant**. You give the value in the declaration, and it can never change. Trying to store a new value in it is an error. Several variables of the same type can share one declaration, separated by commas.

lesson.code:
program circle
  implicit none
  real, parameter :: pi = 3.14159
  real :: radius, area
  radius = 2.0
  area = pi * radius * radius
  print '(A, F0.2)', "Area: ", area
end program circle

lesson.md: All declarations come before the first statement. A declaration after a `print` or after `x = 1` is an error. Without `implicit none`, Fortran guesses the type of an undeclared name from its first letter, so a typo quietly creates a new variable.

card: `'(F0.2)'` for real, `'(L1)'` for logical, `trim(s) // "!"` joins text

units.title: Arithmetic and formatted output
units.summary: Calculate with numbers and powers, learn how integer division works and control the layout of numbers with write and formats.

lesson.md: Fortran calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` (multiply), `/` (divide) and `**` (power). The order is the same as in mathematics: first `**`, then `*` and `/`, then `+` and `-`. Parentheses change the order.

lesson.code:
program math
  implicit none
  print '(I0)', 2 + 3 * 4
  print '(I0)', (2 + 3) * 4
  print '(I0)', 2 ** 10
end program math

lesson.md: When both numbers are integers, `/` gives an integer and cuts off the decimal part: `7 / 2` is `3`. `mod(7, 2)` gives the remainder of the division, `1`. When at least one number is real, the result is real: `7.0 / 2` is `3.5`.

lesson.code:
program division
  implicit none
  print '(I0)', 7 / 2
  print '(I0)', mod(7, 2)
  print '(F0.2)', 7.0 / 2
  print '(F0.2)', real(7) / 2
end program division

lesson.md: `real(n)` turns an integer into a real number. `int(x)` turns a real into an integer and cuts off the decimal part. `nint(x)` rounds to the nearest integer. When you store a real value in an integer variable, Fortran also cuts off the decimal part.

lesson.code:
program convert
  implicit none
  integer :: n
  real :: x
  x = 7.8
  n = x
  print '(I0)', n
  print '(I0)', int(x)
  print '(I0)', nint(x)
  print '(F0.1)', real(n) / 2
end program convert

lesson.md: `write(*, '(I5)') n` works like `print '(I5)', n`. The `*` means the screen. Inside a format, each letter code describes one value: `I5` is an integer in 5 characters, aligned to the right. `F8.3` is a real in 8 characters with 3 digits after the decimal point. `1X` adds one space.

lesson.code:
program table
  implicit none
  write(*, '(I5)') 42
  write(*, '(F8.3)') 3.14159
  write(*, '(A, 1X, I0)') "Items:", 12
  write(*, '(3I4)') 1, 20, 300
end program table

lesson.md: A number in front of a letter code repeats it: `3I4` is the same as `I4, I4, I4`. When a number does not fit into its width, Fortran prints stars instead. `I0` and `F0.2` always use as many characters as the number needs.

lesson.code:
program widths
  implicit none
  write(*, '(I3)') 12345
  write(*, '(I0)') 12345
  write(*, '(A, F0.2, A)') "Weight: ", 9.5, " kg"
end program widths

lesson.md: For numbers between -1 and 1, many compilers, gfortran too, leave out the zero before the decimal point with `F0.2`: `0.5` prints as `.50`. Use a fixed width such as `F4.2` when you want `0.50`.

card: `write(*, '(I5, 1X, F8.3)') n, x` sets the widths

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Run code only when a condition is true with if, else if and select case, and combine conditions with .and., .or. and .not.

lesson.md: `if (condition) then` runs the following lines only when the condition is true. `end if` closes the block. The condition goes in parentheses. You compare values with `==` (equal), `/=` (not equal), `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`.

lesson.code:
program check
  implicit none
  integer :: temp
  temp = 25
  if (temp > 20) then
    print '(A)', "Warm"
  end if
  if (temp /= 25) then
    print '(A)', "Not 25"
  end if
  print '(A)', "Done"
end program check

lesson.md: `else` adds code for the case that the condition is false. `else if` checks another condition. Fortran checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is true.

lesson.code:
program grade
  implicit none
  integer :: score
  score = 72
  if (score >= 90) then
    print '(A)', "A"
  else if (score >= 70) then
    print '(A)', "B"
  else
    print '(A)', "C"
  end if
end program grade

lesson.md: For a single statement there is a short form without `then` and `end if`: `if (x < 0) x = -x` changes `x` only when it is negative.

lesson.code:
program single
  implicit none
  integer :: x
  x = -8
  if (x < 0) x = -x
  print '(I0)', x
end program single

lesson.md: `.and.` is true when both sides are true. `.or.` is true when at least one side is true. `.not.` turns true into false and false into true. A `logical` variable can be a condition on its own. In old code you may see `.eq.`, `.ne.`, `.lt.` and `.gt.` instead of `==`, `/=`, `<` and `>`.

lesson.code:
program logic
  implicit none
  integer :: age
  logical :: member
  age = 15
  member = .true.
  if (age >= 12 .and. age < 18) then
    print '(A)', "Teen"
  end if
  if (age > 65 .or. member) then
    print '(A)', "Discount"
  end if
  if (.not. member) then
    print '(A)', "Guest"
  end if
end program logic

lesson.md: `select case (x)` compares one value with many cases. `case (1)` matches one value, `case (2, 3)` a list, and `case (4:6)` a range from 4 to 6. `case default` matches all other values. It works with integers and texts, but not with real numbers.

lesson.code:
program days
  implicit none
  integer :: day
  day = 6
  select case (day)
  case (1:5)
    print '(A)', "Workday"
  case (6, 7)
    print '(A)', "Weekend"
  case default
    print '(A)', "Unknown"
  end select
end program days

lesson.md: `=` stores a value and `==` compares two values, so `if (x = 5)` is an error. "Not equal" is `/=`, not `!=`, because `!` starts a comment in Fortran.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with do loops and do while, and control loops with exit and cycle.

lesson.md: `do i = 1, 3` … `end do` repeats the lines in between. The **loop variable** `i` must be a declared integer. It starts at `1` and goes up to `3`, and both ends are included.

lesson.code:
program count
  implicit none
  integer :: i
  do i = 1, 3
    print '(A, I0)', "Round ", i
  end do
end program count

lesson.md: A third number sets the **step**: `do i = 0, 10, 5` counts `0`, `5`, `10`. A negative step counts down. When the start is already past the end, the loop runs zero times.

lesson.code:
program steps
  implicit none
  integer :: i
  do i = 0, 10, 5
    print '(I0)', i
  end do
  do i = 3, 1, -1
    print '(I0)', i
  end do
  do i = 5, 1
    print '(A)', "never"
  end do
end program steps

lesson.md: A loop often builds up a result. Here `total` starts at `0`, and each round adds the current value of `i`.

lesson.code:
program sum_up
  implicit none
  integer :: i, total
  total = 0
  do i = 1, 4
    total = total + i
  end do
  print '(A, I0)', "Sum: ", total
end program sum_up

lesson.md: `do while (condition)` repeats as long as the condition is true. Fortran checks the condition before every round, so the loop can also run zero times.

lesson.code:
program doubling
  implicit none
  integer :: n
  n = 1
  do while (n < 50)
    n = n * 2
  end do
  print '(I0)', n
end program doubling

lesson.md: `exit` leaves the loop at once. `cycle` skips the rest of the current round and continues with the next one. A `do` with nothing after it repeats forever, until an `exit` stops it.

lesson.code:
program control
  implicit none
  integer :: i
  do i = 1, 10
    if (mod(i, 2) == 0) cycle
    if (i > 7) exit
    print '(I0)', i
  end do
end program control

program endless
  implicit none
  integer :: n
  n = 0
  do
    n = n + 3
    if (n > 10) exit
  end do
  print '(I0)', n
end program endless

lesson.md: Do not change the loop variable inside a `do i = …` loop: that is an error. In a `do while` loop, make sure that something inside the loop changes the condition, or the loop never ends.

card: `do i = 1, n` … `end do` counts from 1 to n
`do while (x < 100)` repeats while the condition is true
`exit` leaves the loop, `cycle` jumps to the next round

exercises.prompt: What does this print?

total = 0
do i = 2, 8, 3
  total = total + i
end do
print '(I0)', total
exercises.explain: `i` is `2`, `5` and `8`. Their sum is `15`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?

n = 100
steps = 0
do while (n > 1)
  n = n / 2
  steps = steps + 1
end do
print '(I0)', steps
exercises.explain: `n` goes `100`, `50`, `25`, `12`, `6`, `3`, `1`. That is 6 rounds, because integer division cuts off the decimal part.

exercises.prompt: How many times does this print `Hi`?
exercises.code:
integer :: i
do i = 10, 1
  print '(A)', "Hi"
end do
exercises.explain: Without a step, `do` counts up. `10` is already past `1`, so the loop runs zero times.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
integer :: i
do i = 1, 5
  if (i == 3) cycle
  print '(I0)', i
end do
exercises.explain: `cycle` skips the rest of the round when `i` is `3`. The loop then continues with `4` and `5`.

exercises.statement: `exit` ends only the current round, and the loop continues with the next value.
exercises.explain: `exit` leaves the whole loop. `cycle` is the statement that jumps to the next round.

exercises.explain: A step of `-1` counts down by one. With a step of `1`, the loop would run zero times.

units.title: Arrays
units.summary: Store many values in one array, count indexes from 1, work on whole arrays at once and use sum, size and maxval.

lesson.md: An **array** holds many values of the same type under one name. `integer :: scores(3)` declares an array of 3 integers. You reach one element with its **index** in parentheses. The first element is `scores(1)`, not `scores(0)`.

lesson.code:
program first_array
  implicit none
  integer :: scores(3)
  scores(1) = 70
  scores(2) = 85
  scores(3) = 90
  print '(I0)', scores(2)
  print '(I0)', scores(1) + scores(3)
end program first_array

lesson.md: `[3, 1, 4, 1]` creates an array with these values, and older code writes it as `(/ 3, 1, 4, 1 /)`. `size(a)` gives the number of elements. The format `'(*(I0, :, 1X))'` prints all values in one line: `*` repeats the part in parentheses as often as needed, `1X` adds a space, and `:` stops when no values are left, so there is no space after the last number.

lesson.code:
program list
  implicit none
  integer :: a(4)
  a = [3, 1, 4, 1]
  print '(I0)', size(a)
  print '(*(I0, :, 1X))', a
end program list

lesson.md: Calculations work on every element at once: `a * 2` doubles each element, and `a + b` adds two arrays of the same size element by element. `b = 10` stores `10` in every element of `b`.

lesson.code:
program whole
  implicit none
  integer :: a(3), b(3)
  a = [1, 2, 3]
  b = 10
  print '(*(I0, :, 1X))', a * 2
  print '(*(I0, :, 1X))', a + b
end program whole

lesson.md: Fortran has built-in functions for arrays: `sum(a)` adds all elements, `product(a)` multiplies them, and `maxval(a)` and `minval(a)` give the largest and the smallest element.

lesson.code:
program stats
  implicit none
  real :: temps(4)
  temps = [12.0, 15.5, 9.5, 11.0]
  print '(A, F0.1)', "Max: ", maxval(temps)
  print '(A, F0.1)', "Min: ", minval(temps)
  print '(A, F0.2)', "Average: ", sum(temps) / size(temps)
end program stats

lesson.md: A `do` loop from `1` to `size(a)` visits every element. A **slice** such as `a(2:4)` is a part of the array, here the elements 2, 3 and 4. You can use a slice like a small array.

lesson.code:
program slices
  implicit none
  integer :: a(5), i
  a = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
  do i = 1, size(a), 2
    print '(I0)', a(i)
  end do
  print '(*(I0, :, 1X))', a(2:4)
  print '(I0)', sum(a(4:5))
end program slices

lesson.md: An index outside the array, such as `a(0)` or `a(6)` for an array of 5 elements, is an error. Fortran does not always stop with a message: the program may read or change wrong memory, so check your indexes.

card: `integer :: a(5)` has 5 elements, `a(1)` is the first
`a * 2` and `a + b` work on every element
`'(*(I0, :, 1X))'` prints all values in one line

units.title: Functions and subroutines
units.summary: Split a program into functions and subroutines after contains, pass arguments with intent and return results.

lesson.md: A **procedure** is a named block of code that you can run many times. A **subroutine** does a task, and you start it with `call`. You write procedures after the word `contains`, at the end of the program and before `end program`.

lesson.code:
program greet_demo
  implicit none
  call greet("Ada")
  call greet("Alan")
contains
  subroutine greet(name)
    character(len=*), intent(in) :: name
    print '(A)', "Hello, " // name // "!"
  end subroutine greet
end program greet_demo

lesson.md: The values in parentheses are **arguments**. You declare them inside the procedure. `character(len=*)` accepts a text of any length. `intent(in)` says that the procedure only reads the argument and does not change it.

A **function** calculates a value, and you use it inside an expression. `function square(x) result(y)` names the function, its argument `x` and its result variable `y`. You declare `y` inside the function and store the result in it.

lesson.code:
program functions
  implicit none
  print '(I0)', square(4)
  print '(I0)', square(3) + square(2)
contains
  function square(x) result(y)
    integer, intent(in) :: x
    integer :: y
    y = x * x
  end function square
end program functions

lesson.md: A function can take several arguments, separated by commas. Here both arguments and the result are real numbers.

lesson.code:
program average_demo
  implicit none
  real :: a
  a = average(3.0, 4.0)
  print '(F0.2)', a
contains
  function average(x, y) result(m)
    real, intent(in) :: x, y
    real :: m
    m = (x + y) / 2
  end function average
end program average_demo

lesson.md: A subroutine can give values back through its arguments. With `intent(inout)` it reads the argument and may change it. With `intent(out)` it only sets the argument. You pass variables, and after the `call` they hold the new values.

lesson.code:
program swap_demo
  implicit none
  integer :: a, b
  a = 1
  b = 2
  call swap(a, b)
  print '(I0, 1X, I0)', a, b
contains
  subroutine swap(x, y)
    integer, intent(inout) :: x, y
    integer :: tmp
    tmp = x
    x = y
    y = tmp
  end subroutine swap
end program swap_demo

program divide_demo
  implicit none
  integer :: q, r
  call divide(17, 5, q, r)
  print '(A, I0, A, I0)', "17 = 5 * ", q, " + ", r
contains
  subroutine divide(a, b, quotient, remainder)
    integer, intent(in) :: a, b
    integer, intent(out) :: quotient, remainder
    quotient = a / b
    remainder = mod(a, b)
  end subroutine divide
end program divide_demo

lesson.md: Variables that you declare inside a procedure, such as `tmp`, are **local**: they exist only inside that procedure. The `implicit none` of the program also applies to the procedures after `contains`.

Changing an `intent(in)` argument is an error. Do not give a local variable a start value in its declaration, like `integer :: n = 0`, inside a procedure: Fortran sets it only once, not at every call. Use a separate line `n = 0` instead.

card: `function f(x) result(y)` returns the value of `y`

units.title: Derived types and modules
units.summary: Group data in your own derived types, put types and procedures into modules and use them in a program.

lesson.md: A **derived type** groups several values into one new type. You define it with `type :: point` … `end type point`, and each value inside is a **component**. `type(point) :: p` declares a variable of the type, and `%` reaches a component: `p%x`.

lesson.code:
program points
  implicit none
  type :: point
    real :: x
    real :: y
  end type point
  type(point) :: p
  p%x = 1.5
  p%y = 4.0
  print '(F0.1, 1X, F0.1)', p%x, p%y
end program points

lesson.md: `person("Ada", 36)` creates a value with all components, in the order of the type definition. `b = a` copies all components, so changing `b` later does not change `a`.

lesson.code:
program people
  implicit none
  type :: person
    character(len=10) :: name
    integer :: age
  end type person
  type(person) :: a, b
  a = person("Ada", 36)
  b = a
  b%age = b%age + 1
  print '(A, 1X, I0)', trim(a%name), a%age
  print '(A, 1X, I0)', trim(b%name), b%age
end program people

lesson.md: A **module** collects constants, types and procedures, so that many programs can share them. Here the module comes before the program in the same file. In the program, `use geometry` comes right after the `program` line, before `implicit none`.

lesson.code:
module geometry
  implicit none
  real, parameter :: pi = 3.14159
contains
  function circle_area(r) result(a)
    real, intent(in) :: r
    real :: a
    a = pi * r ** 2
  end function circle_area
end module geometry

program shapes
  use geometry
  implicit none
  print '(F0.2)', circle_area(1.0)
  print '(F0.2)', circle_area(2.0)
end program shapes

lesson.md: Types and procedures work well together in a module. Here the subroutine `deposit` takes an `account` and changes its balance.

lesson.code:
module bank
  implicit none
  type :: account
    character(len=10) :: owner
    real :: balance
  end type account
contains
  subroutine deposit(acc, amount)
    type(account), intent(inout) :: acc
    real, intent(in) :: amount
    acc%balance = acc%balance + amount
  end subroutine deposit
end module bank

program banking
  use bank
  implicit none
  type(account) :: acc
  acc = account("Ada", 100.0)
  call deposit(acc, 25.5)
  print '(A, A, F0.2)', trim(acc%owner), ": ", acc%balance
end program banking

lesson.md: `use constants, only: g` makes only the listed names available. In bigger programs this shows clearly where each name comes from.

lesson.code:
module constants
  implicit none
  real, parameter :: g = 9.81
  real, parameter :: c = 299792.458
end module constants

program physics
  use constants, only: g
  implicit none
  print '(F0.2)', g * 2.0
end program physics

lesson.md: In bigger projects, each module goes into its own file, and the compiler translates it before the programs that use it. The order inside a program is always: `use` lines, `implicit none`, declarations, statements, and then `contains` with the procedures.
`use` must come before `implicit none` and before all declarations. Components are reached with `%`, not with a dot: write `p%x`, not `p.x`.

card: `type :: point` … `end type point` defines a type
`type(point) :: p` declares a variable, `p%x` is a component
